cue: How do you say someone put the wrong person in charge?

es.literal: to entrust the sheep to the wolf
es.meaning: To put something in the care of the very person likely to destroy it.
es.example: Lo pusieron a auditar la cuenta que él mismo abrió: encomendar las ovejas al lobo.
es.exampleTranslation: They had him audit the account he opened himself — putting the fox in charge of the henhouse.

it.text: Dare le pecore in custodia al lupo
it.literal: to give the sheep into the wolf's keeping
it.meaning: To put something in the care of the very person likely to destroy it.
it.example: Gli hanno affidato la cassa: dare le pecore in custodia al lupo.
it.exampleTranslation: They put him in charge of the till — the fox minding the henhouse.

bridge.note: Same sheep, same wolf, and a difference in how much machinery each language needs to say entrust. Spanish has a single verb for it, encomendar, and the sentence is done. Italian builds it out of parts — dare in custodia, give into keeping — three words where Spanish uses one, which is the reverse of the usual direction between these two languages. Both are also quietly resisting English, which abandoned the sheep entirely and put a fox in charge of a henhouse.

interference.es_to_it: 'Raccomandare le pecore al lupo' does not work — raccomandare is a false friend here, meaning to recommend or to entrust in a much weaker sense. Italian needs the periphrasis: dare in custodia, or affidare.
interference.it_to_es: Spanish compresses. 'Dar las ovejas en custodia al lobo' is understandable but heavy; the fixed form uses encomendar, a verb Italian has no single equivalent for.
